bathos: A ludicrous descent from the elevated to the low, in writing or speech; anticlimax.
baccarat: A French game of cards, played by a banker and punters.
baldachin: 1. A rich brocade; baudekin. (old) 2. (Arch.) A structure in form of a canopy, sometimes supported by columns, and sometimes suspended from the roof or projecting from the wall; generally placed over an altar; as, the baldachin in St. Peter's. 3. A portable canopy borne over shrines, etc., in procession. [Written also baldachino, baldaquin, etc.]
balcony: 1. (Arch.) A platform projecting from the wall of a building, usually resting on brackets or consoles, and inclosed by a parapet; as, a balcony in front of a window. Also, a projecting gallery in places of amusement; as, the balcony in a theater. 2. A projecting gallery once common at the stern of large ships.
battledoor: 1. An instrument, with a handle and a flat part covered with parchment or crossed with catgut, used to strike a shuttlecock in play; also, the play of battledoor and shuttlecock. 2. Etym: [OE. battleder.] A child's hornbook. (old) Halliwell.
barbarousness: The quality or state of being barbarous; barbarity; barbarism.
backsight: The reading of the leveling staff in its unchanged position when the leveling instrument has been taken to a new position; a sight directed backwards to a station previously occupied. Cf. Foresight, n., 3.
bawsin: 1. A badger. (old) B. Jonson. 2. A large, unwieldy person. (old) Nares.
backslide: To slide back; to fall away; esp. to abandon gradually the faith and practice of a religion that has been professed.
bastardize: 1. To make or prove to be a bastard; to stigmatize as a bastard; to declare or decide legally to be illegitimate. The law is so indulgent as not to bastardize the child, if born, though not begotten, in lawful wedlock. Blackstone. 2. To beget out of wedlock. Shak.
babyhood: The state or period of infancy.
battue: (a) The act of beating the woods, bushes, etc., for game. (b) The game itself. (c) The wanton slaughter of game. Howitt.
basic: 1. (Chem.) (a) Relating to a base; performing the office of a base in a salt. (b) Having the base in excess, or the amount of the base atomically greater than that of the acid, or exceeding in proportion that of the related neutral salt. (c) Apparently alkaline, as certain normal salts which exhibit alkaline reactions with test paper. 2.
barehead: Having the head uncovered; as, a bareheaded girl.
backboard: 1. A board which supports the back wen one is sitting; Note: specifically, the board athwart the after part of a boat. 2. A board serving as the back part of anything, as of a wagon. 3. A thin stuff used for the backs of framed pictures, mirrors, etc. 4.
bargainor: One who makes a bargain, or contracts with another; esp., one who sells, or contracts to sell, property to another. Blackstone.
batman: A weight used in the East, varying according to the locality; in Turkey, the greater batman is about 157 pounds, the lesser only a fourth of this; at Aleppo and Smyrna, the batman is 17 pounds. | A man who has charge of a bathorse and his load. Macaulay.
bacterioscopic: Relating to bacterioscopy; as, a bacterioscopic examination.
basined: Inclosed in a basin. "Basined rivers." Young.
batrachomyomachy: The battle between the frogs and mice; -- a Greek parody on the Iliad, of uncertain authorship.
banality: Something commonplace, hackneyed, or trivial; the commonplace, in speech. The highest things were thus brought down to the banalities of discourse. J. Morley.
banjorine: A kind of banjo, with a short neck, tuned a fourth higher than the common banjo; -- popularly so called.
bamboozler: A swindler; one who deceives by trickery. [Colloq.] Arbuthnot.
bastile: 1. (Feud. Fort.) A tower or an elevated work, used for the defense, or in the siege, of a fortified place. The high bastiles . . . which overtopped the walls. Holland. 2. "The Bastille", formerly a castle or fortress in Paris, used as a prison, especially for political offenders; hence, a rhetorical name for a prison.
bawson: 1. A badger. (old) B. Jonson. 2. A large, unwieldy person. (old) Nares.
babingtonite: A mineral occurring in triclinic crystals approaching pyroxene in angle, and of a greenish black color. It is a silicate of iron, manganese, and lime.
balefire: A signal fire; an alarm fire. Sweet Teviot! on thy silver tide The glaring balefires blaze no more. Sir W. Scott.
bardish: Pertaining to, or written by, a bard or bards. "Bardish impostures." Selden.
backwards: 1. With the back in advance or foremost; as, to ride backward. 2. Toward the back; toward the rear; as, to throw the arms backward. 3. On the back, or with the back downward. Thou wilt fall backward. Shak. 4. Toward, or in, past time or events; ago. Some reigns backward. Locke. 5. By way of reflection; reflexively. Sir J. Davies. 6.
bacchus: The god of wine, son of Jupiter and Semele.
barbiers: A variety of paralysis, peculiar to India and the Malabar coast; -- considered by many to be the same as beriberi in chronic form.
bacillus: A variety of bacterium; a microscopic, rod-shaped vegetable organism.
bastardy: 1. The state of being a bastard; illegitimacy. 2. The procreation of a bastard child. Wharton.
barse: The common perch. See 1st Bass. [Prov. Eng.] Halliwell.
backbite: To wound by clandestine detraction; to censure meanly or spitefully (as absent person); to slander or speak evil of (one absent). Spenser. | To censure or revile the absent. They are arrant knaves, and will backbite. Shak.
balm: 1. (Bot.) An aromatic plant of the genus Melissa. 2. The resinous and aromatic exudation of certain trees or shrubs. Dryden. 3. Any fragrant ointment. Shak. 4. Anything that heals or that mitigates… | To anoint with balm, or with anything medicinal. Hence: To soothe; to mitigate. (old) Shak.
barrulet: A diminutive of the bar, having one fourth its width.
bark: 1. To strip the bark from; to peel. 2. To abrade or rub off any outer covering from; as to bark one's heel. 3. To girdle. See Girdle, v. t., 3. 4. To cover or inclose with bark, or as with bark; | 1. To make a short, loud, explosive noise with the vocal organs; -- said of some animals, but especially of dogs. 2. To make a clamor; to make importunate outcries.
bayoustate: Mississippi; -- a nickname, from its numerous bayous.
baudekin: The richest kind of stuff used in garments in the Middle Ages, the web being gold, and the woof silk, with embroidery : -- made originally at Bagdad. [Spelt also baudkin, baudkyn, bawdekin, and baldakin.] Nares.
baptization: Baptism. (old) Their baptizations were null. Jer. Taylor.
baggagemaster: One who has charge of the baggage at a railway station or upon a line of public travel. [U.S.]
bantling: A young or small child; an infant. [Slightly contemptuous or depreciatory.] In what out of the way corners genius produces her bantlings. W. Irving.
bacharach: A kind of wine made at Bacharach on the Rhine.
bagworm: One of several lepidopterous insects which construct, in the larval state, a baglike case which they carry about for protection. One species (Platoeceticus Gloveri) feeds on the orange tree. See Basket worm.
bash: To abash; to disconcert or be disconcerted or put out of countenance. (old) His countenance was bold and bashed not. Spenser.
backbiting: Secret slander; detraction. Backbiting, and bearing of false witness. Piers Plowman.
baggala: A two-masted Arab or Indian trading vessel, used in Indian Ocean.
backwoodsman: A men living in the forest in or beyond the new settlements, especially on the western frontiers of the older portions of the United States. Fisher Ames.
ballistics: The science or art of hurling missile weapons by the use of an engine. Whewell.
bagman: A commercial traveler; one employed to solicit orders for manufacturers and tradesmen. Thackeray.
baffler: One who, or that which, baffles.
barmote: A court held in Derbyshire, in England, for deciding controversies between miners. Blount.
balmoral: 1. A long woolen petticoat, worn immediately under the dress. 2. A kind of stout walking shoe, laced in front. A man who uses his balmorals to tread on your toes. George Eliot.
barmy: Full of barm or froth; in a ferment. "Barmy beer." Dryden. | Full of barm or froth; in a ferment. "Barmy beer." Dryden.
barruly: Traversed by barrulets or small bars; -- said of the field.
basidiospore: A spore borne by a basidium. -- Ba*sid`i*o*spor"ous (, a.
battalia: 1. Order of battle; disposition or arrangement of troops (brigades, regiments, battalions, etc.), or of a naval force, for action. A drawing up the armies in battalia. Jer. Taylor. 2. An army in battle array; also, the main battalia or body. (old) Shak.
basswood: The bass (Tilia) or its wood; especially, T. Americana. See Bass, the lime tree. All the bowls were made of basswood, White and polished very smoothly. Longfellow.
basipodite: The basal joint of the legs of Crustacea.
balkingly: In manner to balk or frustrate.
banksided: Having sides inclining inwards, as a ship; -- opposed to wall- sided.
bailee: The person to whom goods are committed in trust, and who has a temporary possession and a qualified property in them, for the purposes of the trust. Blackstone. Note: In penal statutes the word includes those who receive goods for another in good faith. Wharton.
bankrupt: 1. (Old Eng. Low) A trader who secretes himself, or does certain other acts tending to defraud his creditors. Blackstone. 2. A trader who becomes unable to pay his debts; an insolvent trader; | 1. Being a bankrupt or in a condition of bankruptcy; unable to pay, or legally discharged from paying, one's debts; as, a bankrupt merchant. 2. Depleted of money;
backsettler: One living in the back or outlying districts of a community. The English backsettlers of Leinster and Munster. Macaulay.
bathybius: A name given by Prof. Huxley to a gelatinous substance found in mud dredged from the Atlantic and preserved in alcohol. He supposed that it was free living protoplasm, covering a large part of the ocean bed. It is now known that the substance is of chemical, not of organic, origin.
barbarian: 1. A foreigner. [Historical] Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me. 2. | Of, or pertaining to, or resembling, barbarians; rude; uncivilized; barbarous; as, barbarian governments or nations.
backsaw: A saw (as a tenon saw) whose blade is stiffened by an added metallic back.
bayard: 1. Etym: [OF. bayard, baiart, bay horse; bai bay + -ard. See Bay, a., and -ard.] Properly, a bay horse, but often any horse. Commonly in the phrase blind bayard, an old blind horse. Blind bayard moves the mill. Philips. 2. Etym: [Cf. F. bayeur, fr. bayer to gape.] A stupid, clownish fellow. (old) B. Jonson.
barbicel: One of the small hooklike processes on the barbules of feathers.
basilisk: 1. A fabulous serpent, or dragon. The ancients alleged that its hissing would drive away all other serpents, and that its breath, and even its look, was fatal. See Cockatrice. Make me not sighted like the basilisk. Shak. 2. (Zoöl.) A lizard of the genus Basiliscus, belonging to the family Iguanidæ.
barmecidal: Unreal; illusory. "A sort of Barmecidal feast." Hood.
bashibazouk: A soldier belonging to the irregular troops of the Turkish army.
base: 1. Of little, or less than the usual, height; of low growth; as, base shrubs. (old) Shak. 2. Low in place or position. (old) Shak. 3. Of humble birth; or low degree; lowly; mean. | 1. The bottom of anything, considered as its support, or that on which something rests for support; the foundation; as, the base of a statue. "The base of mighty mountains." Prescott. 2.
bandana: 1. A species of silk or cotton handkerchief, having a uniformly dyed ground, usually of red or blue, with white or yellow figures of a circular, lozenge, or other simple form. 2.
basommatophora: A group of Pulmonifera having the eyes at the base of the tentacles, including the common pond snails.
ballistic: 1. Of or pertaining to the ballista, or to the art of hurling stones or missile weapons by means of an engine. 2. Pertaining to projection, or to a projectile. Ballistic pendulum, an instrument consisting of a mass of wood or other material suspended as a pendulum, for measuring the force and velocity of projectiles by means of the arc through which their impact impels it.
babyship: The quality of being a baby; the personality of an infant.
barbule: 1. A very minute barb or beard. Booth. 2. (Zoöl.) One of the processes along the edges of the barbs of a feather, by which adjacent barbs interlock. See Feather.
bailbond: (a) A bond or obligation given by a prisoner and his surety, to insure the prisoner's appearance in court, at the return of the writ. (b) Special bail in court to abide the judgment. Bouvier.
battlement: (a) One of the solid upright parts of a parapet in ancient fortifications. (b) pl. The whole parapet, consisting of alternate solids and open spaces. At first purely a military feature, afterwards copied on a smaller scale with decorative features, as for churches.
baraesthesiometer: An instrument for determining the delicacy of the sense of pressure. -- Bar`æs*the`si*o*met"ric, Bar`es*the`si*o*met"ric (#), a.
ballet: 1. An artistic dance performed as a theatrical entertainment, or an interlude, by a number of persons, usually women. Sometimes, a scene accompanied by pantomime and dancing. 2. The company of persons who perform the ballet. 3. (Mus.) A light part song, or madrigal, with a fa la burden or chorus, -- most common with the Elizabethan madrigal composers. 4.
bailiwick: The precincts within which a bailiff has jurisdiction; the limits of a bailiff's authority.
banquetter: One who banquets; one who feasts or makes feasts.
bafta: A coarse stuff, usually of cotton, originally made in India. Also, an imitation of this fabric made for export.
barbarize: 1. To become barbarous. The Roman empire was barbarizing rapidly from the time of Trajan. De Quincey. 2. To adopt a foreign or barbarous mode of speech. The ill habit . . . | To make barbarous. The hideous changes which have barbarized France. Burke.
barleycorn: 1. A grain or "corn" of barley. 2. Formerly , a measure of length, equal to the average length of a grain of barley; the third part of an inch. John Barleycorn, a humorous personification of barley as the source of malt liquor or whisky.
baenomere: One of the somites (arthromeres) that make up the thorax of Arthropods. Packard.
basipterygium: A bar of cartilage at the base of the embryonic fins of some fishes. It develops into the metapterygium. -- Ba*sip`ter*yg"i*al (, a.
bakehouse: A house for baking; a bakery.
bannition: The act of expulsion.(old) Abp. Laud.
batture: An elevated river bed or sea bed.
bachelorism: Bachelorhood; also, a manner or peculiarity belonging to bachelors. W. Irving. BACHELOR'S BUTTON Bach"e*lor's but"ton , (Bot.) A plant with flowers shaped like buttons; especially, several species of Ranunculus, and the cornflower (Centaures cyanus) and globe amaranth (Gomphrena).
badaud: A person given to idle observation of everything, with wonder or astonishment; a credulous or gossipy idler. A host of stories . . . dealing chiefly with the subject of his great wealth, an ever delightful topic to the badauds of Paris. Pall Mall Mag.
bashaw: 1. A Turkish title of honor, now written pasha. See Pasha. 2. Fig.: A magnate or grandee. 3. (Zoöl.) A very large siluroid fish (Leptops olivaris) of the Mississippi valley; -- also called goujon, mud cat, and yellow cat.
banian: 1. A Hindoo trader, merchant, cashier, or money changer. [Written also banyan.] 2. A man's loose gown, like that worn by the Banians. 3. (Bot.) The Indian fig. See Banyan. Banian days (Naut.), days in which the sailors have no flesh meat served out to them. This use seems to be borrowed from the Banians or Banya race, who eat no flesh.
bazaar: 1. In the East, an exchange, marketplace, or assemblage of shops where goods are exposed for sale. 2. A spacious hall or suite of rooms for the sale of goods, as at a fair. 3. A fair for the sale of fancy wares, toys, etc., commonly for a charitable objects. Macaulay.
baggager: One who takes care of baggage; a camp follower. (old) Sir W. Raleigh.
banquette: 1. (Fort.) A raised way or foot bank, running along the inside of a parapet, on which musketeers stand to fire upon the enemy. 2. (Arch.) A narrow window seat; a raised shelf at the back or the top of a buffet or dresser.
barbastel: A European bat (Barbastellus communis), with hairy lips.
bagreef: The lower reef of fore and aft sails; also, the upper reef of topsails. Ham. Nav. Encyc.
barong: A kind of cutting weapon with a thick back and thin razorlike edge, used by the Moros of the Philippine Islands.
barnburner: A member of the radical section of the Democratic party in New York, about the middle of the 19th century, which was hostile to extension of slavery, public debts, corporate privileges, etc., and supported Van Buren against Cass for president in 1848; --opposed to Hunker. [Political Cant, U. S.]
bacchanalia: 1. (Myth.) A feast or an orgy in honor of Bacchus. 2. Hence: A drunken feast; drunken reveler.
bawd: A person who keeps a house of prostitution, or procures women for a lewd purpose; a procurer or procuress; a lewd person; -- usually applied to a woman. | To procure women for lewd purposes.
bacillar: Shaped like a rod or staff.
balladry: Ballad poems; the subject or style of ballads. "Base balladry is so beloved." Drayton.
bankruptcy: 1. The state of being actually or legally bankrupt. 2. The act or process of becoming a bankrupt. 3. Complete loss; -- followed by of.
balsamation: 1. The act of imparting balsamic properties. 2. The art or process of embalming.
barklouse: An insect of the family Coccidæ, which infests the bark of trees and vines. Note: The wingless females assume the shape of scales. The bark louse of vine is Pulvinaria innumerabilis; that of the pear is Lecanium pyri. See Orange scale.
banlieue: The territory without the walls, but within the legal limits, of a town or city. Brande & C.
basilic: 1. Royal; kingly; also, basilican. 2. (Anat.) Pertaining to certain parts, anciently supposed to have a specially important function in the animal economy, as the middle vein of the right arm.
baresthesiometer: An instrument for determining the delicacy of the sense of pressure. -- Bar`æs*the`si*o*met"ric, Bar`es*the`si*o*met"ric (#), a.
babyfarm: A place where the nourishment and care of babies are offered for hire.
baybolt: A bolt with a barbed shank.
bargeman: The man who manages a barge, or one of the crew of a barge.
baffling: Frustrating; discomfiting; disconcerting; as, baffling currents, winds, tasks. -- Bafflingly, adv. -- Bafflingness, n.
barillet: A little cask, or something resembling one. Smart.
bankbook: A book kept by a depositor, in which an officer of a bank enters the debits and credits of the depositor's account with the bank.
baken: p. p. of Bake. [Obs. or. Archaic]
babiism: The doctrine of a modern religious pantheistical sect in Persia, which was founded, about 1844, by Mirza Ali Mohammed ibn Rabhik (1820 -- 1850), who assumed the title of Bab-ed-Din (Per., Gate of the Faith). Babism is a mixture of Mohammedan, Christian, Jewish, and Parsi elements.
badderlocks: A large black seaweed (Alaria esculenta) sometimes eaten in Europe; -- also called murlins, honeyware, and henware.
backing: 1. The act of moving backward, or of putting or moving anything backward. 2. That which is behind, and forms the back of, anything, usually giving strength or stability. 3. Support or aid given to a person or cause. 4. (Bookbinding) The preparation of the back of a book with glue, etc., before putting on the cover.
baptistery: (a) In early times, a separate building, usually polygonal, used for baptismal services. Small churches were often changed into baptisteries when larger churches were built near. (b) A part of a church containing a font and used for baptismal services.
basanite: Lydian stone, or black jasper, a variety of siliceous or flinty slate, of a grayish or bluish black color. It is employed to test the purity of gold, the amount of alloy being indicated by the color left on the stone when rubbed by the metal.
basshorn: A modification of the bassoon, much deeper in tone.
bassorin: A constituent part of a species of gum from Bassora, as also of gum tragacanth and some gum resins. It is one of the amyloses. Ure.
barrowist: A follower of Henry Barrowe, one of the founders of Independency or Congregationalism in England. Barrowe was executed for nonconformity in 1953.
bandon: Disposal; control; license. (old) Rom. of R.
baguette: 1. (Arch.) A small molding, like the astragal, but smaller; a bead. 2. (Zoöl) One of the minute bodies seen in the divided nucleoli of some Infusoria after conjugation.
baccalaureate: 1. The degree of bachelor of arts. (B.A. or A.B.), the first or lowest academical degree conferred by universities and colleges. 2. A baccalaureate sermon. [U.S.] | Pertaining to a bachelor of arts. Baccalaureate sermon, in some American colleges, a sermon delivered as a farewell discourse to a graduating class.
barkingirons: 1. Instruments used in taking off the bark of trees. Gardner. 2. A pair of pistols. [Slang]
bandanna: 1. A species of silk or cotton handkerchief, having a uniformly dyed ground, usually of red or blue, with white or yellow figures of a circular, lozenge, or other simple form. 2.
bagwig: A wig, in use in the 18th century, with the hair at the back of the head in a bag.
barbisonschool: A French school of the middle of the 19th century centering in the village of Barbizon near the forest of Fontainebleau. Its members went straight to nature in disregard of academic tradition, treating their subjects faithfully and with poetic feeling for color, light, and atmosphere. It is exemplified, esp. in landscapes, by Corot, Rousseau, Daubigny, Jules Dupré, and Diaz.
barracuda: 1. (Zoöl.) A voracious pikelike, marine fish, of the genus Sphyræna, sometimes used as food. Note: That of Europe and our Atlantic coast is Sphyræna spet (or S. vulgaris); a southern species is S. picuda; the Californian is S. argentea. 2. (Zoöl.) A large edible fresh-water fish of Australia and New Zealand (Thyrsites atun).
bang: 1. To beat, as with a club or cudgel; to treat with violence; to handle roughly. The desperate tempest hath so banged the Turks. Shak. 2. To beat or thump, or to cause ( something) to hit or strike… | To make a loud noise, as if with a blow or succession of blows; as, the window blind banged and waked me; he was banging on the piano.
bare: 1. Without clothes or covering; stripped of the usual covering; naked; as, his body is bare; the trees are bare. 2. With head uncovered; bareheaded. When once thy foot enters the church, be bare. | 1. Surface; body; substance. You have touched the very bare of naked truth. Marston. 2. (Arch.) That part of a roofing slate, shingle, tile, or metal plate, which is exposed to the weather.
barrier: 1. (Fort.) A carpentry obstruction, stockade, or other obstacle made in a passage in order to stop an enemy. 2. A fortress or fortified town, on the frontier of a country, commanding an avenue of approach. 3. pl. A fence or railing to mark the limits of a place, or to keep back a crowd. No sooner were the barriers opened, than he paced into the lists. Sir W. Scott. 4.
barbarism: 1. An uncivilized state or condition; rudeness of manners; ignorance of arts, learning, and literature; barbarousness. Prescott. 2. A barbarous, cruel, or brutal action; an outrage. A heinous barbarism . . . against the honor of marriage. Milton. 3. An offense against purity of style or language; any form of speech contrary to the pure idioms of a particular language.
badge: 1. A distinctive mark, token, sign, or cognizance, worn on the person; as, the badge of a society; the badge of a policeman. "Tax gatherers, recognized by their official badges. " Prescott. 2. | To mark or distinguish with a badge.
backfire: (a) A fire started ahead of a forest or prairie fire to burn only against the wind, so that when the two fires meet both must go out for lack of fuel. (b) A premature explosion in the cylinder of a gas or oil engine during the exhaust or the compression stroke, tending to drive the piston in a direction reverse to that in which it should travel;
balladmonger: A seller or maker of ballads; a poetaster. Shak.
bathygraphic: Descriptive of the ocean depth; as, a bathygraphic chart.
bayman: In the United States navy, a sick-bay nurse; -- now officially designated as hospital apprentice.
bandelet: A small band or fillet; any little band or flat molding, compassing a column, like a ring. Gwilt.
bagging: 1. Cloth or other material for bags. 2. The act of putting anything into, or as into, a bag. 3. The act of swelling; swelling. | Reaping peas, beans, wheat, etc., with a chopping stroke. [Eng.]
barky: Covered with, or containing, bark. "The barky fingers of the elm." Shak.
bailiff: 1. Originally, a person put in charge of something especially, a chief officer, magistrate, or keeper, as of a county, town, hundred, or castle; one to whom power Abbott. Lausanne is under the canton of Berne, governed by a bailiff sent every three years from the senate. Addison. 2. (Eng. Law) A sheriff's deputy, appointed to make arrests, collect fines, summon juries, etc.
batatas: An aboriginal American name for the sweet potato (Ipomæa batatas).
balbuties: The defect of stammering; also, a kind of incomplete pronunciation.
barbary: The countries on the north coast of Africa from Egypt to the Atlantic. Hence: A Barbary horse; a barb. (old) Also, a kind of pigeon. Barbary ape (Zoöl.), an ape (Macacus innus) of north Africa and Gibraltar Rock, being the only monkey inhabiting Europe. It is very commonly trained by showmen.
baroscopical: Pertaining to, or determined by, the baroscope.
bane: 1. That which destroys life, esp. poison of a deadly quality. [Obs. except in combination, as in ratsbane, henbane, etc.] 2. Destruction; death. (old) The cup of deception spiced and tempered to… | To be the bane of; to ruin. (old) Fuller.
bathometer: An instrument for measuring depths, esp. one for taking soundings without a sounding line.
baron: 1. A title or degree of nobility; originally, the possessor of a fief, who had feudal tenants under him; in modern times, in France and Germany, a nobleman next in rank below a count; in England, a nobleman of the lowest grade in the House of Lords, being next below a viscount.
bayou: An inlet from the Gulf of Mexico, from a lake, or from a large river, sometimes sluggish, sometimes without perceptible movement except from tide and wind. [Southern U. S.] A dark slender thread of a bayou moves loiteringly northeastward into a swamp of huge cypresses. G. W. Cable.
bast: 1. The inner fibrous bark of various plants; esp. of the lime tree; hence, matting, cordage, etc., made therefrom. 2. A thick mat or hassock. See 2d Bass, 2.
batterer: One who, or that which, batters.
baldeagle: The white-headed eagle (Haliæetus leucocephalus) of America. The young, until several years old, lack the white feathers on the head. Note: The bald eagle is represented in the coat of arms, and on the coins, of the United States.
baneful: Having poisonous qualities; deadly; destructive; injurious; noxious; pernicious. "Baneful hemlock." Garth. "Baneful wrath." Chapman. -- Bane"ful*ly, adv. --Bane"ful*ness, n.
batata: An aboriginal American name for the sweet potato (Ipomæa batatas).
balanoid: Resembling an acorn; -- applied to a group of barnacles having shells shaped like acorns. See Acornshell, and Barnacle.
bandrol: A little banner, flag, or streamer. [Written also bannerol.] From the extremity of which fluttered a small banderole or streamer bearing a cross. Sir W. Scott.
baptizable: Capable of being baptized; fit to be baptized. Baxter.
barite: Native sulphate of barium, a mineral occurring in transparent, colorless, white to yellow crystals (generally tabular), also in granular form, and in compact massive forms resembling marble. It has a high specific gravity, and hence is often called heavy spar. It is a common mineral in metallic veins.
baccate: Pulpy throughout, like a berry; -- said of fruits. Gray.
barbiton: An ancient Greek instrument resembling a lyre.
bald: 1. Destitute of the natural or common covering on the head or top, as of hair, feathers, foliage, trees, etc.; as, a bald head; a bald oak. On the bald top of an eminence. Wordsworth. 2. babbler: 1. An idle talker; an irrational prater; a teller of secrets. Great babblers, or talkers, are not fit for trust. L'Estrange. 2. A hound too noisy on finding a good scent. 3. (Zoöl.) A name given to any one of family (Timalinæ) of thrushlike birds, having a chattering note.
basicerite: The second joint of the antennæ of crustaceans.
batta: Extra pay; esp. an extra allowance to an English officer serving in India. Whitworth. | Rate of exchange; also, the discount on uncurrent coins. [India]
backfall: A fall or throw on the back in wrestling.
backlog: A large stick of wood, forming the of a fire on the hearth. [U.S.] There was first a backlog, from fifteen to four and twenty inches in diameter and five feet long, imbedded in the ashes. S. G. Goodrich.
baleful: 1. Full of deadly or pernicious influence; destructive. "Baleful enemies." Shak. Four infernal rivers that disgorge Into the burning lake their baleful streams. Milton. 2. Full of grief or sorrow; woeful; sad. (old)
backward: 1. With the back in advance or foremost; as, to ride backward. 2. Toward the back; toward the rear; as, to throw the arms backward. 3. On the back, or with the back downward. ballahou: A fast-sailing schooner, used in the Bermudas and West Indies.
basihyal: Noting two small bones, forming the body of the inverted hyoid arch.
bandoleer: 1. A broad leather belt formerly worn by soldiers over the right shoulder and across the breast under the left arm. (old)
basicslag: A by-product from the manufacture of steel by the basic process, used as a fertilizer. It is rich in lime and contains 14 to 20 per cent of phosphoric acid. Called also Thomas slag, phosphatic slag, and odorless phosphate.
baysalt: Salt which has been obtained from sea water, by evaporation in shallow pits or basins, by the heat of the sun; the large crystalline salt of commerce. Bacon. Ure.
backhandedness: State of being backhanded; the using of backhanded or indirect methods.
barony: 1. The fee or domain of a baron; the lordship, dignity, or rank of a baron. 2. In Ireland, a territorial division, corresponding nearly to the English hundred, and supposed to have been originally the district of a native chief. There are 252 of these baronies. In Scotland, an extensive freehold. It may be held by a commoner. Brande & C.
baignoire: A box of the lowest tier in a theater. Du Maurier.
bailie: An officer in Scotland, whose office formerly corresponded to that of sheriff, but now corresponds to that of an English alderman.
bakery: 1. The trade of a baker. 2. The place for baking bread; a bakehouse.
baffle: 1. To cause to undergo a disgraceful punishment, as a recreant knight. batfish: A name given to several species of fishes: (a) The Malthe vespertilio of the Atlantic coast. (b) The flying gurnard of the Atlantic (Cephalacanthus spinarella). (c) The California batfish or sting ray (Myliobatis Californicus.)
barretter: A thermal cymoscope which operates by increased resistance when subjected to the influence of electric waves. The original form consisted of an extremely fine platinum wire loop attached to terminals and inclosed in a small glass or silver bulb. In a later variety, called the liquid barretter, wire is replace by a column of liquid in a very fine capillary tube.
bandingplane: A plane used for cutting out grooves and inlaying strings and bands in straight and circular work.
barkbound: Prevented from growing, by having the bark too firm or close.
basketry: The art of making baskets; also, baskets, taken collectively.
backsheesh: In Egypt and the Turkish empire, a gratuity; a "tip".
bavin: 1. A fagot of brushwood, or other light combustible matter, for kindling fires; refuse of brushwood. [Obs. or Dial. Eng.] 2. Impure limestone. [Prov. Eng.] Wright.
bayantler: The second tine of a stag's horn. See under Antler.
bassoon: A wind instrument of the double reed kind, furnished with holes, which are stopped by the fingers, and by keys, as in flutes. It forms the natural bass to the oboe, clarinet, etc. Note: Its compass comprehends three octaves. For convenience of carriage it is divided into two parts; whence it is also called a fagot.
basifugal: Tending or proceeding away from the base; as, a basifugal growth.
battery: 1. The act of battering or beating. 2. (Law) The unlawful beating of another. It includes every willful, angry and violent, or negligent touching of another's person or clothes, or anything attached to his person or held by him. 3. (Mil.) (a) Any place where cannon or mortars are mounted, for attack or defense. (b) Two or more pieces of artillery in the field.
ballista: An ancient military engine, in the form of a crossbow, used for hurling large missiles.
backbiter: One who backbites; a secret calumniator or detractor.
bailey: 1. The outer wall of a feudal castle. (old) 2. The space immediately within the outer wall of a castle or fortress. (old) 3. A prison or court of justice; -- used in certain proper names; as, the Old Bailey in London; the New Bailey in Manchester. [Eng.] Oxf. Gloss.
balneal: Of or pertaining to a bath. Howell.
barkbeetle: A small beetle of many species (family Scolytidæ), which in the larval state bores under or in the bark of trees, often doing great damage.
ballahoo: A fast-sailing schooner, used in the Bermudas and West Indies.
barbette: A mound of earth or a platform in a fortification, on which guns are mounted to fire over the parapet. En barbette, In barbette, said of guns when they are elevated so as to fire over the top of a parapet, and not through embrasures. -- Barbette gun, or Barbette battery, a single gun, or a number of guns, mounted in barbette, or partially protected by a parapet or turret.
baculine: Of or pertaining to the rod or punishment with the rod.
bannock: A kind of cake or bread, in shape flat and roundish, commonly made of oatmeal or barley meal and baked on an iron plate, or griddle; -- used in Scotland and the northern counties of England. Jamieson. Bannock fluke, the turbot. [Scot.]

barry: , Divided into bars; -- said of the field.
basketful: As much as a basket will contain.
barothermograph: An instrument for recording both pressure and temperature, as of the atmosphere.
barramundi: (a) A remarkable Australian fresh-water ganoid fish of the genus Ceratodus. (b) An Australian river fish (Osteoglossum Leichhardtii).
barnstormer: An itinerant theatrical player who plays in barns when a theatre is lacking; hence, an inferior actor, or one who plays in the country away from the larger cities. --Barn"storm`ing, n. [Theatrical Cant]

basilicon: An ointment composed of wax, pitch, resin, and olive oil, lard, or other fatty substance.

baseburner: A furnace or stove in which the fuel is contained in a hopper or chamber, and is fed to the fire as the lower stratum is consumed.
balisaur: A badgerlike animal of India (Arcionyx collaris).
bacchic: Of or relating to Bacchus; hence, jovial, or riotous,with intoxication.
backlash: The distance through which one part of connected machinery, as a wheel, piston, or screw, can be moved without moving the connected parts, resulting from looseness in fitting or from wear; also, the jarring or reflex motion caused in badly fitting machinery by irregularities in velocity or a reverse of motion.
basilar: 1. Relating to, or situated at, the base. 2. Lower; inferior; applied to impulses or springs of action. "Basilar instincts." H. W. Beecher.
bakerlegged: Having legs that bend inward at the knees.
bankside: The slope of a bank, especially of the bank of a steam.
backshish: In Egypt and the Turkish empire, a gratuity; a "tip".
ballroom: A room for balls or dancing.
baseborn: 1. Born out of wedlock. Gay. 2. Born of low parentage. 3. Vile; mean. "Thy baseborn heart." Shak.
barnyard: A yard belonging to a barn.
bardism: The system of bards; the learning and maxims of bards.
baff: A blow; a stroke. [Scot.] H. Miller.
ballooning: 1. The art or practice of managing balloons or voyaging in them. 2. (Stock Exchange) The process of temporarily raising the value of a stock, as by fictitious sales. [U.S.]
barmecide: One who proffers some illusory advantage or benefit. Also used as an adj.: Barmecidal. "A Barmecide feast." Dickens.
banxring: An East Indian insectivorous mammal of the genus Tupaia.
backbond: An instrument which, in conjunction with another making an absolute disposition, constitutes a trust.
batfowler: One who practices or finds sport in batfowling.
bac: 1. A broad, flatbottomed ferryboat, usually worked by a rope. 2. A vat or cistern. See 1st Back.
basbleu: A bluestocking; a literary woman. [Somewhat derisive]
bantamwork: Carved and painted work in imitation of Japan ware.
balistraria: A narrow opening, often cruciform, through which arrows might be discharged.
batteler: A student at Oxford who is supplied with provisions from the buttery; formerly, one who paid for nothing but what he called for, answering nearly to a sizar at Cambridge. Wright.
basquish: Pertaining to the country, people, or language of Biscay; Basque (old) Sir T. Browne.
barwood: A red wood of a leguminous tree (Baphia nitida), from Angola and the Gaboon in Africa. It is used as a dyewood, and also for ramrods, violin bows and turner's work.
baboon: One of the Old World Quadrumana, of the genera Cynocephalus and Papio; the dog-faced ape. Baboons have dog-like muzzles and large canine teeth, cheek pouches, a short tail, and naked callosities on the buttocks. They are mostly African. See Mandrill, and Chacma, and Drill an ape.
banner: 1. A kind of flag attached to a spear or pike by a crosspiece, and used by a chief as his standard in battle. Hang out our banners on the outward walls. Shak. 2. A large piece of silk or other cloth, with a device or motto, extended on a crosspiece, and borne in a procession, or suspended in some conspicuous place. 3. Any flag or standard; as, the star-spangled banner.
balancereef: The last reef in a fore-and-aft sail, taken to steady the ship.
baroscope: Any instrument showing the changes in the weight of the atmosphere; also, less appropriately, any instrument that indicates - or foreshadows changes of the weather, as a deep vial of liquid holding in suspension some substance which rises and falls with atmospheric changes.
battleship: An armor-plated man-of-war built of steel and heavily armed, generally having from ten thousand to fifteen thousand tons displacement, and intended to be fit to meet the heaviest ships in line of battle.
bandmaster: The conductor of a musical band.
bargainer: One who makes a bargain; -- sometimes in the sense of bargainor.
bathing: Act of taking a bath or baths. Bathing machine, a small room on wheels, to be driven into the water, for the convenience of bathers, who undress and dress therein.
banana: A perennial herbaceous plant of almost treelike size (Musa sapientum); also, its edible fruit. See Musa. bab: Lit., gate; -- a title given to the founder of Babism, and taken from that of Bab-ud-Din, assumed by him.
bale: A bundle or package of goods in a cloth cover, and corded for storage or transportation; also, a bundle of straw Bale of dice, a pair of dice. (old) B. Jonson. | To make up in a bale. Goldsmith.
babel: 1. The city and tower in the land of Shinar, where the confusion of languages took place. Therefore is the name of it called Babel. Gen. xi. 9. 2. Hence: A place or scene of noise and confusion; a confused mixture of sounds, as of voices or languages. That babel of strange heathen languages. Hammond. The grinding babel of the street. R. L. Stevenson.
baldrib: A piece of pork cut lower down than the sparerib, and destitute of fat. [Eng.] Southey.
bawl: 1. To cry out with a loud, full sound; to cry with vehemence, as in calling or exultation; to shout; to vociferate. 2. To cry loudly, as a child from pain or vexation. | To proclaim with a loud voice, or by outcry, as a hawker or town-crier does. Swift.
banco: A bank, especially that of Venice. Note: This term is used in some parts of Europe to indicate bank money, as distinguished from the current money, when this last has become depreciated.
babble: 1. To utter words indistinctly or unintelligibly; to utter inarticulate sounds; as a child babbles. 2. To talk incoherently; to utter unmeaning words. 3. barkeeper: One who keeps or tends a bar for the sale of liquors.
batoidei: The division of fishes which includes the rays and skates.
bacon: The back and sides of a pig salted and smoked; formerly, the flesh of a pig salted or fresh. Bacon beetle (Zoöl.), a beetle (Dermestes lardarius) which, especially in the larval state, feeds upon bacon, woolens, furs, etc. See Dermestes. -- To save one's bacon, to save one's self or property from harm or less. [Colloq.]
baptism: The act of baptizing; the application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ceremony, by which he is initiated into the visible church of Christ. This is performed by immersion, sprinkling, or pouring.
bathymetrical: Pertaining to bathymetry; relating to the measurement of depths, especially of depths in the sea.
barpost: A post sunk in the ground to receive the bars closing a passage into a field.
bascinet: A light helmet, at first open, but later made with a visor. [Written also basinet, bassinet, basnet.]
barbizonschool: A French school of the middle of the 19th century centering in the village of Barbizon near the forest of Fontainebleau. Its members went straight to nature in disregard of academic tradition, treating their subjects faithfully and with poetic feeling for color, light, and atmosphere. It is exemplified, esp. in landscapes, by Corot, Rousseau, Daubigny, Jules Dupré, and Diaz.
batiste: Originally, cambric or lawn of fine linen; now applied also to cloth of similar texture made of cotton.
baal: 1. (Myth.) The supreme male divinity of the Phoenician and Canaanitish nations. Note: The name of this god occurs in the Old Testament and elsewhere with qualifying epithets subjoined, answering to the different ideas of his character; as, Baal-berith (the Covenant Baal), Baal-zebub (Baal of the fly). 2. pl. The whole class of divinities to whom the name Baal was applied.
bailor: One who delivers goods or money to another in trust.
bancal: An ornamental covering, as of carpet or leather, for a bench or form.
badian: An evergreen Chinese shrub of the Magnolia family (Illicium anisatum), and its aromatic seeds; Chinese anise; star anise.
backsword: 1. A sword with one sharp edge. 2. In England, a stick with a basket handle, used in rustic amusements; also, the game in which the stick is used. Also called singlestick. Halliwell.
bandlet: A small band or fillet; any little band or flat molding, compassing a column, like a ring. Gwilt.
barrow: 1. A support having handles, and with or without a wheel, on which heavy or bulky things can be transported by hand. See Handbarrow, and Wheelbarrow. 2. (Salt Works) A wicker case, in which salt is… | A hog, esp. a male hog castrated. Holland.
bartlett: A Bartlett pear, a favorite kind of pear, which originated in England about 1770, and was called Williams' Bonchrétien. It was brought to America, and distributed by Mr. Enoch Bartlett, of Dorchester, Massachusetts.
battailant: Prepared for battle; combatant; warlike. Spenser. -- n. A combatant. Shelton.

barbaric: 1. Of, or from, barbarian nations; foreign; -- often with reference to barbarous nations of east. "Barbaric pearl and gold." Milton. 2. Of or pertaining to, or resembling, an uncivilized person or people; barbarous; barbarian; destitute of refinement. "Wild, barbaric music." Sir W. Scott.
batprinting: A mode of printing on glazed ware.
battler: A student at Oxford who is supplied with provisions from the buttery; formerly, one who paid for nothing but what he called for, answering nearly to a sizar at Cambridge. Wright.
bailer: 1. One who bails or lades. 2. A utensil, as a bucket or cup, used in bailing; a machine for bailing water out of a pit.
batting: 1. The act of one who bats; the management of a bat in playing games of ball. Mason. 2. Cotton in sheets, prepared for use in making quilts, etc.; as, cotton batting.

backwardation: The seller's postponement of delivery of stock or shares, with the consent of the buyer, upon payment of a premium to the latter; -- also, the premium so paid. See Contango. Biddle.
bareheaded: Having the head uncovered; as, a bareheaded girl.
badigeon: A cement or paste (as of plaster and freestone, or of sawdust and glue or lime) used by sculptors, builders, and workers in wood or stone, to fill holes, cover defects, or finish a surface.
balneotherapy: The treatment of disease by baths.
bacterium: A microscopic vegetable organism, belonging to the class Algæ, usually in the form of a jointed rodlike filament, and found in putrefying organic infusions. babyfarmer: One who keeps a baby farm.
baronage: 1. The whole body of barons or peers. The baronage of the kingdom. Bp. Burnet. 2. The dignity or rank of a baron. 3. The land which gives title to a baron. (old)
basely: 1. In a base manner; with despicable meanness; dishonorably; shamefully. 2. Illegitimately; in bastardy. (old) Knolles.
backside: The hinder part, posteriors, or rump of a person or animal. Note: Backside (one word) was formerly used of the rear part or side of any thing or place, but in such senses is now two words.
bating: With the exception of; excepting. We have little reason to think that they bring many ideas with them, bating some faint ideas of hunger and thirst. Locke.
balachong: A condiment formed of small fishes or shrimps, pounded up with salt and spices, and then dried. It is much esteemed in China.
baccara: A French game of cards, played by a banker and punters.
